assessment.summary: Documented AI harms keep accumulating as adoption widens — nearly 18,000 incidents and hazards logged by the OECD's monitor — and governments are extending risk frameworks to critical infrastructure; the severe tail, misuse at scale or loss of control, stays debated but is treated as a real risk by governments and intergovernmental bodies.
assessment.timeframe: Capabilities and adoption are advancing rapidly and documented incidents are rising; expert estimates of severe global outcomes span a very wide range.

claims.text: The total number of AI incidents and hazards reported in public media surged between 2022 and 2025, per OECD analysis of the OECD.AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM).

Media-reported AI incidents and hazards linked to synthetic media, child safety, and cyberattacks and fraud have more than doubled since 2022 (OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 53, February 2026).

NIST released the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) on 26 January 2023 to help manage risks to individuals, organizations, and society associated with artificial intelligence, and released a Generative AI Profile (NIST-AI-600-1) on 26 July 2024.

The OECD AI Incidents Monitor (AIM) documents approximately 16,894 AI incidents and hazards in total; the platform notes that incidents have gotten more media attention lately, but have actually gone down as a share of all AI news.
The OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM) reports a running total of about 17,930 incidents and hazards.

On April 7, 2026, NIST released a concept note for an AI RMF Profile on Trustworthy AI in Critical Infrastructure, intended to guide critical infrastructure operators towards specific risk management practices when engaging AI-enabled capabilities; NIST also states that the AI RMF 1.0 is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan.

published.description: Risks from increasingly capable, widely deployed AI systems: present-day harms such as synthetic media, fraud and cyberattacks, plus contested scenarios of large-scale misuse or loss of control. The OECD's AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor has now logged about 17,930 documented incidents and hazards, roughly a thousand more than in August 2026, with the categories tied to synthetic media, child safety and cyber-fraud having more than doubled since 2022. Governments and standards bodies are widening their frameworks in step: NIST issued a concept note in April 2026 for an AI Risk Management Framework profile covering critical infrastructure, and is revising the framework itself under the White House AI Action Plan. Quantified estimates of the severe tail remain scarce by nature.
published.name: Advanced AI Risk

assessment.summary: Measured AMOC change is real but contested: a reconstructed slowdown of about 15 percent since the 1950s and a 12% weakening of the deep Antarctic Bottom Water limb over 2000-2020, set against NOAA's finding that the overturning weakening has nearly stalled since the early 2010s and that the Florida Current has held steady for 40 years. An outright collapse this century is a low-probability, high-impact tail that EU risk bodies now treat as a security planning problem rather than a forecast, and for which early warning monitoring does not yet exist.
assessment.timeframe: Direct basin-wide monitoring spans only about two decades, so the observed trend remains uncertain; an abrupt collapse is generally assessed as unlikely this century, but would be effectively irreversible on human timescales if it occurred.

claims.text: NOAA's Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory describes the AMOC as the Atlantic component of the global ocean conveyor belt and a crucial component of the global heat, salt, nutrients and carbon balances in the ocean, affecting regional climate, sea level and marine ecosystems.
NOAA reports that extensive weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation occurred in the 2000s, primarily driven by anthropogenic forcing (increased CO2 and reduced aerosol).

NOAA reports that a strengthening natural signal since the early 2010s has cancelled out the anthropogenic weakening signal, leading to a near stalling of the AMOC weakening, and that the Florida Current has remained remarkably stable over the past 40 years.
A study reported by NOAA's Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory found that the northward transport of Antarctic Bottom Water at 16°N weakened by about 12% during 2000-2020.
NOAA Fisheries reported in 2018 that a reconstruction of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation indicates it has slowed down or weakened by about 15 percent since the 1950s.

A January 2025 European Commission Joint Research Centre policy brief states that widespread and systemic risks of crossing several Earth System Tipping Points are becoming an emerging security threat for Europe, naming a collapse of the Atlantic ocean circulation as an example with direct impacts to Europe, and calls for early warning monitoring systems and tipping-point-tailored risk assessments for Europe.

published.description: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation carries warm water northward through the Atlantic, and a collapse of it would abruptly reorganise climate across Europe and the tropics. NOAA describes the AMOC as the Atlantic component of the global ocean conveyor belt and a crucial component of the global heat, salt, nutrients and carbon balances in the ocean. Whether it is already failing is genuinely contested: NOAA Fisheries reported in 2018 a slowdown of about 15 percent since the 1950s, and NOAA's Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory found extensive weakening in the 2000s driven primarily by anthropogenic forcing — but also that a natural strengthening signal since the early 2010s has produced a near stalling of that weakening, with the Florida Current remarkably stable over the past 40 years. The deep limb gives a clearer signal: northward transport of Antarctic Bottom Water at 16°N weakened by about 12% during 2000-2020. The policy concern is the tail rather than the trend — the European Commission's Joint Research Centre names a collapse of the Atlantic ocean circulation among the Earth System Tipping Points posing an emerging security threat to Europe.
published.name: Atlantic Overturning Circulation (AMOC) Collapse

assessment.summary: A present, quantified global toll — millions of deaths a year already associated with resistant bacterial infections — that is worsening across most tracked pathogens, with one in six bacterial infections worldwide now resistant to the antibiotics used to treat them and mounting economic cost.
assessment.timeframe: Already underway; resistance rose across more than 40% of tracked pathogen-antibiotic combinations between 2018 and 2023, with costs projected to climb steadily through 2035.

claims.text: Bacterial antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was estimated to be associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021.
The total cost to treat resistant bacterial infections alone is predicted to reach US$ 412 billion annually up to 2035, with additional productivity losses of US$ 443 billion per year.
WHO reports that one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections causing common infections in people worldwide in 2023 were resistant to antibiotic treatments.
WHO reports that between 2018 and 2023, antibiotic resistance rose in over 40% of the pathogen-antibiotic combinations monitored, with an average annual increase of 5-15%.

WHO reports that antibiotic resistance is highest in the WHO South-East Asian and Eastern Mediterranean Regions, where 1 in 3 reported infections were resistant, and in the African Region, where 1 in 5 infections was resistant; the estimates draw on data reported to the Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS) from over 100 countries.

Member States at the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly adopted the updated Global action plan on antimicrobial resistance (GAP-AMR) 2026-2036 on 23 May 2026, developed by the Quadripartite organizations (FAO, UNEP, WHO and WOAH).

published.description: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites evolving resistance to the drugs used to treat them, driven by overuse and misuse of antimicrobials in humans, animals, and agriculture. Unlike a single pandemic pathogen, AMR is a gradual, ongoing erosion of the effectiveness of modern medicine — common infections, surgery, and cancer treatment all become more dangerous as resistance spreads. WHO's global surveillance now puts one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide beyond the reach of the antibiotics used against them, rising to one in three in the South-East Asian and Eastern Mediterranean Regions, and resistance is climbing in more than 40% of the pathogen-antibiotic combinations it tracks. Last-line carbapenems and fluoroquinolones are losing ground against E. coli, K. pneumoniae, Salmonella and Acinetobacter. The policy response is a ten-year global action plan adopted in May 2026, but surveillance itself remains patchy: roughly half of the countries that report to WHO still lack the laboratory systems to generate reliable data.
published.name: Antimicrobial Resistance

assessment.summary: A present, quantified global decline in species and ecosystems — up to a million species threatened with extinction and most of the land and ocean already altered — with cascading risk to the food, water, and climate systems it underpins. IPBES's 2024 assessment found reform-oriented conservation has largely failed to reverse the decline, and its February 2026 business assessment finds finance flows harmful to nature outweighing conservation and restoration spending by more than thirty to one, with under 1% of publicly reporting companies disclosing their biodiversity impacts.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing decline over recent decades, with many losses (species extinctions, ecosystem tipping points) becoming irreversible within decades absent action.

claims.text: Up to 1 million species are threatened with extinction, many within decades, more than ever before in human history (IPBES Global Assessment, 2019).
75 percent of the terrestrial environment has been severely altered to date by human actions, and 66 percent of the marine environment (IPBES Global Assessment, 2019).
The current rate of global species extinction is tens to hundreds of times higher than the average over the last 10 million years, and it is accelerating (IPBES Global Assessment, 2019).

The cost of delaying actions to halt and reverse biodiversity loss and nature's decline around the world by even a decade is estimated to be double that of acting now (IPBES Transformative Change Assessment, approved 18 December 2024 in Windhoek, Namibia).

In 2023, global public and private finance flows with directly negative impacts on nature were estimated at $7.3 trillion, of which private finance accounted for $4.9 trillion, with public spending on environmentally harmful subsidies of about $2.4 trillion (IPBES Business and Biodiversity Assessment, approved at the 12th session of the IPBES Plenary in Manchester, United Kingdom, February 2026).

$220 billion in public and private finance flows were directed in 2023 to activities contributing to the conservation and restoration of biodiversity, representing just 3% of the public funds and incentives that encourage harmful business behaviour or prevent behaviour beneficial to biodiversity (IPBES Business and Biodiversity Assessment, February 2026).

Less than 1% of publicly reporting companies mention their impacts on biodiversity in their reports; the assessment was prepared by 79 leading experts from 35 countries and approved by representatives of the more than 150 member Governments of IPBES (IPBES Business and Biodiversity Assessment, February 2026).

published.description: An accelerating, human-driven decline in species and ecosystems that underpin food, water, and climate stability. Nature is being altered at a global scale and pace unprecedented in human history, with a growing share of the ecosystem services humanity depends on already in decline. IPBES's 2024 Transformative Change Assessment found that reform-oriented conservation has largely failed to halt or reverse this decline, and that delaying corrective action by even a decade roughly doubles its eventual cost. Its Business and Biodiversity Assessment, approved in February 2026, traces how the money still runs the other way: in 2023 roughly $7.3 trillion of public and private finance flows had directly negative impacts on nature, against $220 billion directed to conservation and restoration, while under 1% of publicly reporting companies disclose their biodiversity impacts at all.
published.name: Biodiversity Loss and Ecosystem Collapse

assessment.summary: Recorded attacks fall overwhelmingly on the sectors governments designate as critical — 73 percent of organisations targeted across the EU in 2025 were essential or important entities under NIS2, public administration most of all. Volume is dominated by low-impact denial-of-service while ransomware does the most short-term damage; the tail risk is an attack severe enough to disable critical infrastructure across multiple countries at once, made more plausible by shared supply-chain and cloud dependencies.
assessment.timeframe: Incident volume is tracked annually; a severe multi-country outage could occur at any time given uneven critical-infrastructure protection and shared supply-chain and cloud dependencies.

claims.text: 139 countries have active Computer Incident Response Teams, with various levels of sophistication, up from 109 in the 2021 index, and 132 countries have a National Cybersecurity Strategy as of 2024, up from 107 in 2021 (ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024).

Worrisome threats highlighted in the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024 include ransomware attacks targeting government services and other sectors, cyber breaches affecting core industries, costly system outages, and breaches of privacy for individuals and organizations.

NIST released version 2.0 of its Cybersecurity Framework on 26 February 2024; the framework was originally developed in 2014 to help protect critical infrastructure such as hospitals and power plants, and CSF 2.0 expands its scope to organizations in any sector.

NIST's National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence published Special Publication 1800-45, Cybersecurity for the Water and Wastewater Sector: Build Architecture, on 24 June 2026, demonstrating how water utilities of different sizes can securely enable remote access to operational technology as the sector adopts more internet-connected sensors, data collection, network devices, and analytic software.

ENISA's Threat Landscape 2026, published on 22 September 2026 and covering incidents observed from 1 January to 31 December 2025, found that 73 percent of the targeted organisations are essential and important entities under the NIS2 Directive, with public administration the most targeted sector in 32 percent of cases.

In ENISA's Threat Landscape 2026, low-impact distributed denial-of-service attacks accounted for 51 percent of recorded cases, while ransomware remains the most short-term impactful type of incident; the report's central finding is that cyber dependencies — including supply chains, third-party providers and cloud services — expand the attack surface.

published.description: A cyberattack severe enough to disable power grids, financial systems, water utilities, or other critical infrastructure across a wide area. Attacks already concentrate on those sectors: ENISA found 73 percent of organisations targeted across the EU during 2025 were “essential” or “important” entities under the NIS2 Directive — the categories covering energy, water, transport, health and public administration — with public administration the most targeted sector at 32 percent of cases. Most of that volume was low-impact denial-of-service (51 percent of recorded cases), while ransomware remained the most short-term impactful incident type, and ENISA's central finding was that dependencies on supply chains, third-party providers and cloud services widen the attack surface beyond what any one defender controls. National protections are rising but uneven: 139 countries run active incident-response teams and 132 have a national cybersecurity strategy. NIST issued practice guidance in June 2026 for securing remote access to water and wastewater operational technology.
published.name: Large-Scale Cyberattack on Critical Infrastructure

assessment.summary: A present, quantified concentration risk — a single country supplies the U.S. with a major share of over a third of the minerals it most depends on importing, and the value of U.S. net imports of processed metals and materials more than doubled in a single year — that has already produced real supply shocks and price spikes, with escalation to a broader multi-country industrial disruption a live risk.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing and worsening; the U.S. critical minerals list and import-reliance figures are reassessed annually, and 2025 saw China's export controls disrupt automaker production, cut indium export volumes sharply, and double the value of U.S. processed-mineral imports.

claims.text: The U.S. remained reliant on imports from China as a major source for 14 of the 33 critical minerals for which the United States most depends on imports (USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026).

Net imports of processed metals and materials more than doubled by value, from $77 billion in 2024 to $185 billion in 2025, and the Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 covers 14 minerals, from antimony to tungsten, that China restricts exporting to the United States (USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026).

The Department of the Interior's final 2025 List of Critical Minerals, published November 6, 2025 by USGS, identifies 60 minerals vital to the U.S. economy and national security whose supply chains face potential disruption risk, adding 10 new minerals — including copper, silver, and uranium — to the list.

China is the leading global producer of indium, accounting for 70% of the world total; the United States recovered no indium from ores in 2025 and its net import reliance was 100% of estimated consumption (USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, February 2026).

In February 2025, China's Ministry of Commerce subjected several critical minerals, including indium, to new export restrictions; USGS reports Asian Metal data showing that exports of unwrought indium declined by 72%, year over year, from September 2024 to September 2025 (USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, February 2026).

published.description: The energy, defense, and technology sectors depend on a small set of minerals whose mining and, especially, refining are concentrated in a handful of countries. Export restrictions, geopolitical tension, or a shock to a single dominant supplier can disrupt processed-material flows worldwide with little substitution available in the short term, as China's 2025 export controls on rare earths and antimony already demonstrated by forcing automakers to cut production and sending prices sharply higher. Indium shows the pattern in miniature: China produces 70% of world supply, the United States recovered none from its own ores in 2025, and unwrought indium exports fell 72% year over year after Beijing added the metal to its February 2025 restrictions.
published.name: Critical Mineral Supply Chain Disruption

assessment.summary: Extreme (Carrington-class) storms are rare but historically documented, while the severe storms below that level recur many times per solar cycle; modern grid, satellite, and GPS dependence makes a repeat event far more disruptive than in 1859 or 1989, with credible multi-trillion-dollar damage estimates from U.S. federal sources.
assessment.timeframe: NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center issues routine G1-G4 storm watches and warnings, and its scales put G5 (Extreme) conditions at roughly 4 events per solar cycle; the largest historical events cluster once every few decades to a century, with no reliable long-range prediction of the next one.

claims.text: The 1859 Carrington Event, the largest geomagnetic storm in recorded history, crippled a large portion of the telegraph system across North America and Europe, with operators reporting fires from sparking equipment; on 13 March 1989, a severe geomagnetic storm took the Hydro-Québec electricity transmission system offline, leaving six million people without power for nine hours, many for days.

Citing the National Academies of Sciences, NOAA states that a Carrington-magnitude solar storm today has the potential to cost nearly $2 trillion, disrupting telecommunications, banking systems, GPS, and the energy grid, with an estimated 20-40 million people in the United States at risk of extended power outages lasting from 16 days to 1-2 years.

NOAA estimates the economic value of impacts to the U.S. electric power industry from a single geomagnetic storm event could range from $100 million for a small event up to $27 billion (2019 dollars) for a very large but unlikely event, and that a Carrington-level event could cause direct domestic economic damage of approximately $1.2 trillion over five months, with global impacts of $2.4 to $3.4 trillion over one year.

The NOAA Space Weather Scales give an average frequency of 100 G4 (Severe) geomagnetic storms per solar cycle (60 days per cycle) and 4 G5 (Extreme) storms per solar cycle (4 days per cycle). At G5, NOAA states that 'some grid systems may experience complete collapse or blackouts', transformers 'may experience damage', pipeline currents 'can reach hundreds of amps', HF radio propagation 'may be impossible in many areas for one to two days', and satellite navigation 'may be degraded for days'.

published.description: A severe solar eruption can drive strong electrical currents through Earth's surface, threatening power grids, satellites, GPS, radio, and aviation communications over a wide area. The 1859 Carrington Event, the largest geomagnetic storm on record, crippled telegraph systems across North America and Europe, and a March 1989 storm knocked out Hydro-Quebec's grid, leaving six million people without power for nine hours. Storms of moderate severity are routine rather than rare: NOAA's Space Weather Scales put the average frequency at about 100 G4 (Severe) storms per roughly 11-year solar cycle, and 4 G5 (Extreme) storms, at which grid systems may collapse and transformers may be damaged. Modern societies are far more dependent on the electronics and satellite systems such storms disrupt, and NOAA cites a National Academies of Sciences estimate that a Carrington-level storm today could put 20-40 million people in the United States at risk of extended power outages lasting from 16 days to 1-2 years, with total economic damage estimated at nearly $2 trillion.
published.name: Extreme Geomagnetic Storm (Solar Superstorm)

assessment.summary: A present, quantified toll of hundreds of thousands of conflict-related deaths a year across dozens of countries; overall fatalities eased slightly in 2025 but stayed higher than any other year since 2018, while the number of interstate conflicts doubled. Civilian harm in the largest of those wars has kept rising through 2026, with Ukraine's January-August civilian casualties 55% above the same period in 2025.
assessment.timeframe: Chronic and ongoing, with conflict-related fatalities near a multi-year high, interstate armed conflict having doubled in 2025, and civilian casualties in Ukraine climbing through 2026.

claims.text: The overall estimated number of conflict-related fatalities reduced slightly, by 4.2 per cent, from 249,000 in 2024 to 238,000 in 2025 — still higher than any other year in the period 2018-25 (SIPRI Yearbook 2026).

There were five major armed conflicts in 2025 (involving over 10,000 conflict-related fatalities each), one more than in 2024, while the number of high-intensity conflicts (1,000-9,999 fatalities) fell from 23 in 2024 to 20 in 2025 (SIPRI Yearbook 2026).

The number of interstate armed conflicts doubled from three in 2024 to six in 2025, involving at least 13 states, while the number of states with armed conflict on their territory fell slightly from 50 in 2024 to 49 in 2025 (SIPRI Yearbook 2026).

Civilian casualties in Ukraine from January to August 2026 (2,222 killed; 13,058 injured) were 55 per cent higher than in the same period in 2025 and more than double the same period in 2024; at least 372 civilians were killed and 2,349 injured in August 2026 alone, the second highest monthly figure of the year after July (448 killed; 2,675 injured) (OHCHR Protection of Civilians in Armed Conflict - August 2026, published 16 September 2026).

published.description: Ongoing state-based and civil wars that already kill hundreds of thousands of people a year and displace tens of millions more. Conflict-related fatalities eased slightly in 2025 but stayed above every other year since 2018, while the number of interstate armed conflicts doubled to six, involving at least 13 states. Ukraine, the largest interstate war among them, has intensified further: more civilians were killed and injured there in the first eight months of 2026 than in the whole of 2025, with long-range missile and drone attacks the leading cause. Escalation, spillover between neighbouring conflicts, and breakdown of humanitarian norms are the primary pathways to wider regional or global instability.
published.name: Global Armed Conflict

assessment.summary: A present, quantified global strain — 645 million hungry and 2.1 billion food-insecure in 2025, billions water-insecure — easing slowly on the hunger side for a third year running, while food prices climb again and the escalation pathways still run through climate extremes and conflict.
assessment.timeframe: Chronic and ongoing; acute regional food crises recur annually, and climate change intensifies water stress through mid-century.

claims.text: An estimated 8.2 percent of the global population, about 673 million people, experienced hunger in 2024 (FAO, The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2025).
The global prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity was 28.0 percent in 2024, accounting for 2.3 billion people (FAO SOFI 2025).
266 million people are facing crisis levels of hunger or worse, according to the Global Report on Food Crises.
Roughly half of the world's population experiences severe water scarcity for at least part of the year (UN World Water Development Report 2024).
As of 2022, 2.2 billion people were without access to safely managed drinking water (UN World Water Development Report 2024).

The FAO Food Price Index averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, up 0.6 percent from its June level and 1.0 percent higher than its year-earlier level, with the Vegetable Oil Price Index reaching its highest level since June 2022.

An estimated 645 million people (7.8 percent of the global population) faced hunger in 2025, nearly 14 million fewer than in 2024 and 43 million fewer than at the 2022 peak; approximately 2.1 billion people experienced moderate or severe food insecurity in 2025, nearly 86 million fewer than a year earlier (FAO, The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026, launched 21 July 2026).

SOFI 2026 projects that around 520 million people could still face hunger in 2030, putting the world off track to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger); approximately 309 million people in Africa remain undernourished, where hunger prevalence fell from 20.3 percent in 2024 to 20.0 percent in 2025.

The FAO Food Price Index averaged 133.3 points in August 2026, up 2.5 points (1.9 percent) from its revised July level, with all commodity groups recording higher price indices than in the previous month; the index stood 3.3 points (2.5 percent) above its year-earlier level but 26.9 points (16.8 percent) below its March 2022 peak (released 4 September 2026).

published.description: A chronic global shortfall in access to adequate food and safe freshwater, driven by conflict, economic shocks, and climate extremes. Hunger has now eased for three consecutive years — an estimated 645 million people, 7.8 percent of the world, went hungry in 2025, and 2.1 billion faced moderate or severe food insecurity — yet roughly half the world's population still experiences severe water scarcity for part of the year and 2.2 billion lack safely managed drinking water. Food prices are climbing again, with the FAO Food Price Index at 133.3 points in August 2026 on broad-based commodity increases, and FAO projects around 520 million people could still be hungry in 2030. The tail risk is cascading food-system and water-supply failures that destabilize whole regions.
published.name: Global Food and Water Insecurity

assessment.summary: Over a hundred million people remain forcibly displaced worldwide — a standing stress on regional stability and the international protection system. The population edged down for the first time in a decade in 2025 on the back of large-scale returns, but the response is contracting faster: UNHCR's funding fell by a quarter between 2024 and 2025 and it reached only a third of its 2026 appeal by July, putting nearly 8.3 million displaced and stateless people at risk of losing assistance.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing at historic scale; large-scale returns produced the first decline in ten years during 2025, while a 2026 funding shortfall is eroding the protection response faster than the displaced population is falling.

claims.text: At the end of 2025, 117.8 million people worldwide were forcibly displaced — roughly one in every 70 people (UNHCR Global Trends, June 2026). The page's prose gives the ratio (one in every 70 people, 1.4 per cent of the world's population); its 2025 data table gives the components — 67,228,580 internally displaced, 28,461,306 refugees under UNHCR's mandate, 5,964,782 Palestine refugees under UNRWA's mandate, 8,998,091 asylum-seekers and 7,177,473 other people in need of international protection — which sum to 117,830,232.
Global refugee numbers fell by three per cent in 2025 to 41.6 million.
14.7 million displaced people went back to their areas or countries of origin in 2025, including 4.4 million refugees and 10.3 million internally displaced people.
70 per cent of refugees are living in protracted, long-term displacement situations (UNHCR Global Trends briefing, June 2026).

Nearly 8.3 million refugees and other forcibly displaced and stateless people could lose access to vital assistance, according to UNHCR's report Protection Eroded: The Human Cost of Underfunding, published on 29 September 2026.

UNHCR's available funding fell from $5.178 billion in 2024 to $3.932 billion in 2025, and by July 2026 the agency had received 32 per cent of the $8.5 billion it needed for the year; it cut its workforce by a third in 2025 and closed offices in 140 locations.

published.description: Displacement by persecution, conflict, violence, and human-rights violations at near-record scale. 117.8 million people were forcibly displaced at the end of 2025 — roughly one in every 70 people — and 2025 brought the first decline in a decade, driven by 14.7 million returns, of which 4.4 million were refugees; even so, 70 percent of refugees remain in protracted situations. What is changing faster than the caseload is the capacity to respond. UNHCR's available funding fell from $5.178 billion in 2024 to $3.932 billion in 2025, and by July 2026 it had received 32 percent of the $8.5 billion it needed for the year; it cut its workforce by a third during 2025 and closed offices in 140 locations. Its September 2026 assessment puts nearly 8.3 million refugees and other forcibly displaced and stateless people at risk of losing access to vital assistance — a widening protection gap behind a slowly falling headline number.
published.name: Global Forced Displacement Crisis

assessment.summary: An ongoing, human-caused warming of the climate system with civilizational-scale risks under continued high emissions; 2026 is tracking among the warmest years on record while atmospheric CO2 continues to rise.
assessment.timeframe: Already underway; impacts intensify with cumulative emissions.

claims.text: The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report attributes approximately 1.1 °C of global warming since 1850-1900 to human activities.

NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information ranked 2025 as the third-warmest year in the global temperature record dating back to 1850: the annual global surface temperature was 2.11°F (1.17°C) above the 20th-century average and 2.41°F (1.34°C) above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average, behind only 2024 and 2023. The ten warmest years in the 176-year record have all occurred since 2015, and upper-ocean heat content was record high in 2025.
NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory measured a monthly mean atmospheric CO2 concentration of 431.44 ppm at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii in June 2026, up from 429.61 ppm in June 2025.

NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information reported that global surface temperatures in July 2026 were 2.12°F (1.18°C) above the 20th-century average, tying with 2024 for the warmest July on record, and that the January-July global surface temperature was the third highest on record. NCEI's annual outlook states it is very likely that 2026 will rank among the five-warmest years on record, with the highest probabilities favoring it as the third- or fourth-warmest.

published.description: Sustained warming of Earth's climate system driven by human greenhouse-gas emissions, with widespread impacts on weather extremes, sea level, ecosystems, and human systems. Unlike discrete events, it is an ongoing, intensifying process: 2025 was the third-warmest year on NOAA's global record, 1.34°C above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average, and the ten warmest years on record have all occurred since 2015. The pace has not slackened in 2026 — July 2026 tied 2024 as the warmest July on record, the January-July global temperature was the third highest on record, and NOAA's annual outlook makes it very likely that 2026 finishes among the five warmest years. Atmospheric CO2 at NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory reached 431.44 ppm in June 2026, up from 429.61 ppm a year earlier and the highest level in over two million years.
published.name: Climate Change (Global Warming)

assessment.summary: A recurrent biological threat whose severe-pandemic form could greatly exceed the already-large annual burden of seasonal influenza; the main watch item is H5N1, which kills roughly half of the people it is confirmed to infect but has not acquired sustained human-to-human transmission.
assessment.timeframe: Pandemics recur on the order of every few decades; timing is not predictable.

claims.text: The WHO states seasonal influenza causes 290,000 to 650,000 respiratory deaths annually.
The WHO states there are around a billion cases of seasonal influenza annually worldwide, including 3-5 million cases of severe illness.

WHO's cumulative table of confirmed human cases of avian influenza A(H5N1) reported to WHO for 2003-2026 records 1,002 cases and 479 deaths across 25 reporting countries, with data in WHO headquarters as of 7 August 2026.

WHO states the World Health Assembly adopted the WHO Pandemic Agreement in May 2025, and that at the close of the seventh meeting of the Intergovernmental Working Group on 17 July 2026 member states were still negotiating the agreement's Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing annex, with an eighth meeting scheduled for 14-18 September 2026.

published.description: A novel influenza strain to which the population has little immunity could spread worldwide and cause mortality far exceeding ordinary seasonal influenza, as in 1918. Pandemics have recurred several times per century, and the ordinary seasonal burden — around a billion cases and 290,000 to 650,000 respiratory deaths a year — is the floor a pandemic strain would build on. Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) remains the most closely watched candidate: WHO has logged just over a thousand confirmed human infections since 2003, almost half of them fatal, but these are sporadic cases tied to animal exposure rather than sustained human-to-human transmission. The international response framework is still being completed — the WHO Pandemic Agreement was adopted in May 2025, but its Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing annex, which would govern how samples and countermeasures are shared during a pandemic, is still under negotiation.
published.name: Influenza Pandemic

assessment.summary: A present, quantified decline in the productive capacity of land — 1.56 billion hectares degraded worldwide, including more than 460 million hectares of forest, and roughly 100 million hectares of healthy land lost each year — that is directly cutting crop yields for 1.7 billion people and is slow to reverse. Restoration lags badly behind the damage, and FAO prices the failure to restore at $878 billion to $6.3 trillion a year, 2 to 8.3 percent of global GDP.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing and accumulating; FAO's SDG indicator 15.3.1 series shows degradation still expanding through 2019, with sub-Saharan Africa, Western Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Southern Asia degrading 6 to 8 percent faster than the global average since 2015, while restoration remains far short of the 2030 targets.

claims.text: FAO estimates that 1 660 million hectares of land — more than 10 percent of the world's land area — have been degraded by human activity, with over 60 percent of that degradation occurring on agricultural land, including cropland and pastureland.

Between 2015 and 2019 the world lost at least 100 million hectares of healthy and productive land every year, and these worsening trends impact the lives of 1.3 billion people who are estimated to be directly exposed to land degradation (SDG indicator 15.3.1).

In Eastern Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Central Asia at least 20 percent of total land area was degraded over 2000-2019, while most other regions were over 10 percent; land in sub-Saharan Africa, Western Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Southern Asia is degrading considerably faster than the global average, with increases of 6 percent to 8 percent since 2015.

1.7 billion people live in areas where crop yields have fallen by at least 10 percent due to human-induced land degradation (The State of Food and Agriculture 2025: Addressing land degradation across landholding scales, released 3 November 2025).

FAO's State of the World's Forests 2026, released on 28 September 2026, finds that 1.56 billion hectares of land are degraded globally, and that more than 460 million hectares of forest are degraded worldwide.

91 countries and areas have pledged more than 190 million hectares for forest restoration, but only 206.5 million hectares of forests are currently under restoration (FAO, The State of the World's Forests 2026).

FAO puts the annual cost of failing to restore degraded ecosystems at $878 billion to $6.3 trillion, equivalent to 2 to 8.3 percent of annual GDP, while restoring more than 1 billion hectares of degraded land could generate $1.8 trillion per year in benefits (The State of the World's Forests 2026).

published.description: Land degradation and desertification are the progressive loss of soil productivity and vegetation cover across the world's croplands, pastures, and drylands. FAO's State of the World's Forests 2026 puts degraded land at 1.56 billion hectares globally, including more than 460 million hectares of forest, and over 60 percent of human-induced degradation falls on agricultural land. Between 2015 and 2019 the world lost at least 100 million hectares of healthy, productive land a year, leaving 1.3 billion people directly exposed; 1.7 billion live where crop yields have fallen by at least 10 percent because of it. Restoration is not keeping pace: against pledges of more than 190 million hectares from 91 countries and areas, FAO counts only 206.5 million hectares of forest under restoration, and prices the failure to restore degraded ecosystems at $878 billion to $6.3 trillion a year. Because soil recovers over decades rather than seasons, losses compound rather than reverse.
published.name: Land Degradation and Desertification

assessment.summary: Autonomous weapons are being fielded faster than the law governing them is being written; large General Assembly majorities back new rules, but several states with the most capable systems vote against them. The expert group has closed with a consensus set of agreed elements for an instrument, leaving the November 2026 Review Conference to decide whether negotiations ever start — and an arms race under no binding constraint as the default if they do not.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing, with a decision point in view: the seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons meets at the Palais des Nations in Geneva on 16-20 November 2026, and is where States decide whether to launch negotiations on a legally binding instrument, against a UN and ICRC target of adopting one by the end of 2026.

claims.text: In a renewed joint appeal on 25 August 2026, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said: "We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: the autonomous targeting of humans by machines." The appeal renews a 2023 joint call for States to negotiate a legally binding agreement by 2026 and points to the seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, in Geneva in November 2026, as the clearest path available.

On 1 December 2025 the General Assembly adopted its resolution on lethal autonomous weapons systems (A/C.1/80/L.41) by a recorded vote of 164 in favour to 6 against (Belarus, Burundi, Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Israel, Russian Federation, United States), with 7 abstentions.

On 2 December 2024 the General Assembly adopted its resolution on lethal autonomous weapons systems (A/C.1/79/L.77) by a recorded vote of 166 in favour to 3 against (Belarus, Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Russian Federation), with 15 abstentions, expressing concern about the risk of an emerging arms race, exacerbation of existing conflicts, humanitarian crises and miscalculations, lowering the threshold for an escalation of conflicts and proliferation, including to unauthorized recipients such as non-State actors.

On 14 May 2025 the UN Secretary-General called lethal autonomous weapon systems "politically unacceptable" and "morally repugnant", said that machines with the power and discretion to take human lives without human control should be prohibited by international law, and urged Member States to agree clear regulations and prohibitions by 2026.

At the First Committee's second plenary meeting of the General Assembly's eighty-first session, on 6 October 2026, the Chair said the Group of Governmental Experts on lethal autonomous weapon systems, under the framework of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, "concluded its work with a consensus report"; the High Representative for Disarmament Affairs, Izumi Nakamitsu, cited the agreed elements for an instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems as an achievement showing that the disarmament machinery can adapt to new challenges.

The 7th Review Conference of the High Contracting Parties to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons is scheduled to run from 16 to 20 November 2026 at the Palais des Nations in Geneva, Switzerland.

published.description: Lethal autonomous weapons systems select and engage targets without meaningful human control over the decision to kill. No binding international instrument governs them. The General Assembly has adopted successive resolutions on the subject — 166 to 3 in December 2024, 164 to 6 in December 2025 — but several of the states with the most advanced programmes vote against. The expert group under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons has closed its three-year mandate with a consensus report setting out agreed elements for an instrument it was never mandated to negotiate; whether negotiations open now falls to the Convention's seventh Review Conference, in Geneva on 16-20 November 2026. The Secretary-General and the President of the International Committee of the Red Cross jointly call that conference the clearest path available, warning in August 2026 that the world is dangerously close to crossing a moral red line in the autonomous targeting of humans by machines. The risk is less a single catastrophe than an arms race under no binding constraint that lowers the threshold for using force, compresses escalation below human reaction times, and proliferates to non-State actors.
published.name: Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems

assessment.summary: A recurrent, well-quantified hazard — about 15 magnitude-7 and one magnitude-8+ earthquake expected globally each year, concentrated on the Pacific Ring of Fire — whose worst instances have killed hundreds of thousands of people in a single event, and which no one can predict in advance.
assessment.timeframe: Large earthquakes recur every year worldwide; a single catastrophic event striking a major population center can occur at any time, and short-term prediction remains impossible.

claims.text: According to long-term records since about 1900, USGS expects about 16 major earthquakes worldwide in any given year, including 15 earthquakes in the magnitude 7 range and one earthquake of magnitude 8.0 or greater.
USGS worldwide earthquake statistics record 298,101 deaths from earthquakes in 2004 (the Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami) and 226,050 in 2010, among the deadliest years on record.

USGS states that neither the USGS nor any other scientists have ever predicted a major earthquake, and that USGS scientists can only calculate the probability that a significant earthquake will occur in a specific area within a certain number of years.

USGS states that about 81 percent of the planet's largest earthquakes occur along the Circum-Pacific seismic belt (the Ring of Fire), and that the Alpide belt accounts for about 17 percent of the world's largest earthquakes.

A USGS earthquake catalog query covering 1 January to 21 September 2026 returns a count of 11 earthquakes of magnitude 7.0 or greater worldwide, against the long-term expectation of about 16 major earthquakes per year.

published.description: A large-magnitude earthquake striking a densely populated or poorly prepared region can kill tens to hundreds of thousands of people in seconds and collapse infrastructure across a wide area. Large earthquakes occur every year somewhere on Earth: USGS long-term records since about 1900 give an expectation of roughly 16 major earthquakes annually, 15 in the magnitude 7 range and one of magnitude 8.0 or greater, and the 2026 catalog is running in line with that. The risk is concentrated along active plate boundaries — about 81% of the largest earthquakes occur around the Pacific Ring of Fire and a further 17% along the Alpide belt from the Mediterranean through the Himalayas. What makes the hazard permanent is that it cannot be forecast: USGS states plainly that no scientist has ever predicted a major earthquake, and that only the probability of one in a given area over a span of years can be calculated. Exposure and building standards, not warning, decide the death toll.
published.name: Major Earthquake

assessment.summary: A recurrent, well-catalogued hazard whose historical toll — over 270 deadly tsunamis and more than 544,000 known deaths — is dominated by a handful of basin-wide events, the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami alone killing 227,899 people. Ocean-crossing waves can be warned against hours ahead; locally generated ones arrive within minutes and effectively cannot be, which is why exposure and evacuation readiness, not detection, decide the death toll.
assessment.timeframe: Tsunamis recur throughout the historical record, with over 270 deadly ones catalogued; the basin-wide, mass-casualty events come from great subduction-zone earthquakes that recur on timescales of centuries at any one source and cannot be forecast.

claims.text: Of the approximately 2,800 events in the NCEI Global Historical Tsunami Database, more than 1,400 are confirmed tsunamis. Over 270 confirmed deadly tsunamis have resulted in over 544,000 known (or confirmed) deaths, a number NOAA notes may include deaths from the generating event such as the earthquake.

NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information describe the Global Historical Tsunami Database as spanning 2000 B.C. to the present and including more than 27,000 runup locations where tsunami effects were observed.
NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information record 227,899 deaths from the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, and state that tsunamis have caused more than 500,000 fatalities throughout the world.
In the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, wave heights reached 167 feet in Indonesia's Aceh province, and the waves reached some areas within 20 minutes and others in 7 hours.
NOAA states that landslide-generated tsunamis can impact coastlines within minutes with little to no warning, though they usually lose energy quickly and rarely affect distant coastlines.

USGS states that geologic evidence of submerged vegetation indicates that large or great earthquakes of magnitude 8 to 9 have occurred on average every 500 years along the Cascadia subduction zone, and that a tsunami was generated on 26 January 1700 by a local earthquake close to magnitude 9.

USGS warns that if you see the tsunami, it is too late to out run it, and that future great ruptures of the Cascadia subduction zone would most likely cause local and possibly ocean-wide tsunamis that could affect the western United States.
The US National Weather Service states that a tsunami can strike any ocean coast at any time, and that we cannot predict where, when or how destructive the next tsunami will be.

published.description: A tsunami is a series of ocean waves, usually set off by a large undersea earthquake, that can cross an entire ocean basin and kill tens of thousands of people on arrival. NOAA's global historical database holds approximately 2,800 events back to 2000 B.C., of which more than 1,400 are confirmed tsunamis and over 270 were deadly, together accounting for over 544,000 known deaths — a figure NOAA cautions may include deaths from the generating earthquake. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami alone killed 227,899 people, with wave heights reaching 167 feet in Indonesia's Aceh province and water arriving in some areas within 20 minutes and others only after 7 hours. That spread is the heart of the hazard: distant coasts can be warned, but a locally generated tsunami often outruns any alert, and landslide-driven ones can impact coastlines within minutes with little to no warning. The great subduction-zone sources recur on timescales of centuries — USGS finds magnitude 8 to 9 earthquakes have occurred on average every 500 years on the Cascadia zone, the last on 26 January 1700 — and the National Weather Service states it cannot predict where, when or how destructive the next tsunami will be.
published.name: Major Tsunami

assessment.summary: A rare, high-consequence impact; no known large object currently threatens Earth, though the catalogue of hazardous-size objects is incomplete — fewer than half of the estimated 140-meter-and-larger population has been found.
assessment.timeframe: No known object of concern is on an impact trajectory this century.

claims.text: NASA reports that no known asteroid larger than 140 meters has a significant chance of hitting Earth for the next 100 years.
NASA reports that fewer than half of the estimated 25,000 near-Earth objects 140 meters and larger have been found to date.
With over 90% of the near-Earth objects larger than one kilometer already discovered, NASA's NEO Observations Program is now focusing on finding 90% of the NEO population larger than 140 meters.

NASA raised the 2032 Earth-impact probability of asteroid 2024 YR4 to 3.1% on 18 February 2025, stating that this was 'the highest impact probability NASA has ever recorded for an object of this size or larger'; new data collected overnight reduced the impact probability to 1.5% the following day.

NASA states that asteroid 2024 YR4 poses no significant impact risk to Earth in 2032 and beyond, and that observations by the James Webb Space Telescope on 18 and 26 February ruled out any chance of the asteroid impacting the Moon on 22 December 2032, when it will instead fly by the Moon at a distance of 13,200 miles.

NASA's near-Earth asteroid tally as of 3 December 2025 records 39,123 discovered near-Earth asteroids of all sizes, of which 873 are larger than 1 kilometer with an estimated 50 left to be found, and 11,343 are larger than 140 meters with an estimated 14,000 remaining to be found.

published.description: A sufficiently large near-Earth object striking Earth would cause regional to continental devastation. NASA's Planetary Defense effort catalogues and tracks the larger near-Earth object population to assess impact hazards decades in advance, and reports that no known asteroid larger than 140 meters has a significant chance of hitting Earth for the next 100 years. The catalogue is still incomplete: as of December 2025 NASA counted 39,123 discovered near-Earth asteroids, including 873 larger than 1 kilometer with about 50 left to find, but only 11,343 larger than 140 meters with an estimated 14,000 still undiscovered. The system was tested in 2024-2026 by asteroid 2024 YR4, whose Earth-impact probability peaked at 3.1% in February 2025 — the highest NASA has ever recorded for an object of that size or larger — before follow-up observations, including from the James Webb Space Telescope, ruled out any impact of Earth or the Moon.
published.name: Near-Earth Asteroid Impact

assessment.summary: Extremely rare on any human timescale and with no candidate close enough to threaten Earth — the nearest red supergiant supernova candidate is around 700 light-years away, fourteen times NASA's 50-light-year damage threshold — but a close event could not be prevented and its modelled effect is severe: a Galactic gamma-ray burst at 2 kiloparsecs would cut the ozone column by 35 percent globally and 55 percent at some latitudes for more than five years, with widespread extinctions likely.
assessment.timeframe: No known object threatens Earth. Core-collapse supernovae within 8 parsecs recur about 1.5 times per billion years, gamma-ray bursts close enough to affect Earth about every 15 million years, and Betelgeuse — the nearest red supergiant candidate, around 700 light-years away — is not expected to explode for roughly another 100,000 years.

claims.text: For Earth's ozone layer to experience damage from a supernova, the blast must occur less than 50 light-years away, and all of the nearby stars capable of going supernova are much farther than this. Astronomers estimate that a gamma-ray burst could affect Earth from up to 10,000 light-years away, with each separated by about 15 million years, on average; the closest burst on record, GRB 031203, was 1.3 billion light-years away.

Two-dimensional atmospheric model calculations find that for the combined ozone depletion from supernova gamma rays and cosmic rays roughly to double the "biologically active" UV flux received at the surface of the Earth, the supernova must occur within about 8 parsecs, and that the time-averaged Galactic rate of core-collapse supernovae occurring within 8 pc is 1.5 per billion years; the authors conclude this pathway for mass extinctions "may be less important than previously thought" (Gehrels et al., The Astrophysical Journal 585:1169, 10 March 2003).

Based on cosmological rates, it is probable that at least once in the last billion years the Earth has been irradiated by a gamma-ray burst in our Galaxy from within 2 kpc. A ten second burst delivering 100 kJ/m2 to the Earth results in globally averaged ozone depletion of 35%, with depletion reaching 55% at some latitudes; significant global depletion persists for over 5 years after the burst, and a 50% decrease in ozone column density results in approximately three times the normal UVB flux, making widespread extinctions likely on extrapolation from the UVB sensitivity of modern organisms (Thomas et al., "Terrestrial Ozone Depletion Due to a Milky Way Gamma-Ray Burst").
Betelgeuse, the nearest red supergiant supernova candidate, is around 700 light-years away, and scientists expect its explosion isn't likely to happen for about another 100,000 years.

Modelling of a gamma-ray burst over the South Pole found the resulting ground-level ozone is around 10 parts per billion, below the at least 30 ppb it takes to increase the risk of death due to respiratory failure in humans or to make ozone a risk to vegetation, so that pathway would not have played a part in the Ordovician mass extinction around 450 million years ago (NASA Astrobiology, 8 November 2016).

published.description: A supernova or gamma-ray burst exploding close enough to Earth would strip away much of the ozone layer, exposing the surface to damaging ultraviolet radiation for years. NASA puts the damage threshold for a supernova at under 50 light-years, and every nearby star capable of exploding is far beyond it: Betelgeuse, the closest red supergiant candidate, sits around 700 light-years away and is not expected to explode for roughly another 100,000 years. The modelled consequences of a close event are nonetheless severe. A two-dimensional atmospheric model of a ten-second Galactic gamma-ray burst 2 kiloparsecs away found globally averaged ozone depletion of 35 percent, reaching 55 percent at some latitudes and persisting for over five years — enough, on the authors' extrapolation from the UVB sensitivity of modern organisms, to make widespread extinctions likely. The recurrence rates are what make this a background risk rather than a forecast: core-collapse supernovae within 8 parsecs occur about 1.5 times per billion years, and gamma-ray bursts close enough to affect Earth roughly every 15 million years. Neither can be deflected, and nothing in the current sky is a candidate.
published.name: Nearby Supernova or Gamma-Ray Burst

assessment.summary: Loss of regulatory control over radioactive material is continuous and well documented — hundreds of incidents reported every year, concentrated in industrial and medical sources and in transport, where more than half of all thefts since 1993 and about 70% in the last decade have occurred. The severe tail stays rare: confirmed trafficking intent accounts for a small fraction of thefts, and no seizure of kilogram quantities of weapons-usable nuclear material has been reported since 1994.
assessment.timeframe: Incidents are reported to the IAEA every year, fluctuating around a long-term average of roughly 180 per year; the rare high-consequence case — a radiological dispersal device, or diversion of weapons-usable material — could occur at any time, but the last seizure of kilogram quantities of weapons-usable nuclear material was in 1994.

claims.text: As of 31 December 2025, a total of 4626 incidents have been reported by participating States to the IAEA Incident and Trafficking Database: 359 categorized within Group I (connected or likely connected with trafficking or malicious use), 1120 within Group II (undetermined intent) and 3147 within Group III (not, or unlikely to be, connected with trafficking or malicious use).

In 2025, 236 incidents were reported to the ITDB by 34 States, an increase of 89 incidents from 2024; the IAEA states the increase reflects retrospective reporting of past incidents rather than an actual increase in incident frequency.

Reports to the ITDB have fluctuated around a long-term average of approximately 180 incidents per year since the trend stabilized after 2007, and the database's information is disseminated through the IAEA to 145 participating States, a number that remained unchanged in 2025.

Of all incidents reported to the ITDB, 14% involved nuclear material, 60% involved other radioactive material, and 26% involved radioactively contaminated and other material; the IAEA reports that incidents involving nuclear material continue to decline.

Overall, 54.5% of all thefts reported to the ITDB since 1993 have occurred during the authorized transport of nuclear or other radioactive material, and this figure stands at 69.6% in the last decade.

Of the thefts reported to the ITDB, 3.7% have been confirmed to be related to trafficking, 9.7% have been confirmed not to be related to trafficking or malicious use, and the trafficking or malicious use intent of 86.6% of thefts remains undetermined.

In the period between 1993 and 2025, confirmed Group I incidents included high enriched uranium (13), plutonium (3) and plutonium-beryllium neutron sources (5); the latest incident that involved kilogram quantities of weapons usable nuclear material occurred in 1994.

Thefts of Category 1-3 sealed radioactive sources — those the IAEA classes as dangerous to extremely dangerous to a person — comprise 11.7% of the total stolen sources, while thefts of Category 4 and 5 sources that are unlikely to be dangerous comprise 88.3%.

published.description: Nuclear and radioactive material that slips out of regulatory control could supply the ingredients for a radiological dispersal device or an improvised nuclear device. The IAEA's Incident and Trafficking Database has logged 4,626 incidents reported by participating States since 1993, 236 of them in 2025, though the agency attributes that year's rise mainly to retrospective reporting rather than to more incidents occurring. The overwhelming majority are not malicious: 3,147 incidents sit in the group confirmed or likely unconnected to trafficking, and the intent behind 86.6% of reported thefts is undetermined. What the record shows instead is a chronic regulatory and security weakness — 60% of incidents involve radioactive sources used in industry and medicine, and 54.5% of all thefts since 1993 occurred during authorized transport, rising to 69.6% in the last decade. Weapons-usable material is the rare exception: 13 confirmed high-enriched-uranium cases and 3 plutonium cases across 32 years, and the last seizure of kilogram quantities of weapons-usable nuclear material was in 1994.
published.name: Nuclear and Radiological Material Out of Regulatory Control

assessment.summary: Thousands of warheads remain in military stockpiles — thousands deployed, and roughly two thousand on high alert — making nuclear war a persistent, low-probability, civilization-scale risk, now with no bilateral treaty capping the two largest arsenals since New START lapsed in February 2026.
assessment.timeframe: No reliable forecast; risk tracks geopolitical crises, arsenal modernization, and the erosion or renewal of arms-control agreements — the last US-Russia strategic treaty lapsed in February 2026.

claims.text: SIPRI estimates a total global inventory of 12,187 nuclear warheads in January 2026, of which about 9,745 were in military stockpiles for potential use.

An estimated 4,012 warheads were deployed with missiles and aircraft in January 2026, and between 2,100 and 2,200 of the deployed warheads were kept in a state of high operational alert on ballistic missiles.
Nine states possess nuclear weapons: the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France, China, India, Pakistan, North Korea and Israel.
Russia and the USA together possess around 83 per cent of all stockpiled nuclear warheads.

With the expiry of the bilateral 2010 Treaty on Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms (New START) in February 2026, uncertainty is increasing about the future direction of US and Russian strategic nuclear force levels (SIPRI Yearbook 2026).

published.description: A deliberate or inadvertent nuclear exchange between states. Global arsenals remain in the thousands of warheads — about 9,745 of an estimated 12,187 held in military stockpiles for potential use in January 2026, some 4,012 of them deployed and between 2,100 and 2,200 kept on high operational alert. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their forces, and Russia and the United States alone hold roughly 83 percent of stockpiled warheads. New START, the last bilateral treaty capping their strategic forces, expired in February 2026 with no replacement, leaving the future direction of US and Russian strategic force levels newly uncertain.
published.name: Nuclear War

assessment.summary: A measured, ongoing shift in ocean chemistry — surface pH already down about 0.1 unit since pre-industrial times, roughly a 30% rise in acidity — projected to fall a further 0.3–0.4 units by 2100, eroding the calcifying species at the base of marine food webs and the fisheries built on them.
assessment.timeframe: Already underway and directly measured in ocean time series; the projected additional 0.3–0.4 pH decline runs to 2100, and surface-ocean chemistry takes thousands of years to recover once emissions stop.

claims.text: NOAA's Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory states that the ocean's pH at the sea surface once measured at 8.2 before the 1700s and today is estimated at 8.1, a 0.1 decrease in ocean pH.

NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory states that since the Industrial Revolution the global average pH of the surface ocean has decreased by 0.11, which corresponds to approximately a 30% increase in hydrogen ion concentration.
The Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO states that every year the ocean absorbs about 25% of human-made carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions.

NOAA Fisheries states that over the past 200 years the world's oceans have absorbed more than 150 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emitted from human activities, and that ocean carbon dioxide concentrations are now higher than at any time during the past 800,000 years.
NOAA states that by 2100 the average pH of the ocean's surface waters could decrease by 0.3 to 0.4, a 100% to 150% increase in acidification over the next 75 years.

NOAA states that the predicted pH decrease of approximately 0.3 units during the 21st century would be a greater change than possibly at any time in the last 300 million years, and that when aragonite saturation state falls below 3 calcifying organisms become stressed, while below 1 shells and other aragonite structures begin to dissolve.

NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory reports that oyster seed production in the U.S. Northwest plummeted by as much as 80 percent between 2005 and 2009 as acidified water reached hatcheries, in a Washington shellfish industry worth $270 million a year.

published.description: Ocean acidification is the measured fall in seawater pH caused by the ocean absorbing about a quarter of human carbon dioxide emissions. Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, raising the hydrogen-ion concentration and stripping out the carbonate ions that corals, oysters, clams, pteropods and other calcifying organisms need to build shells and skeletons. Surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 before the 1700s to about 8.1 today — roughly a 30% rise in acidity — and NOAA projects a further decline of 0.3–0.4 units by 2100 on current emissions, a shift larger than possibly any in the last 300 million years. This is not a discrete disaster but a slow, near-irreversible change in the chemistry of the entire ocean: it does not threaten human survival directly, and it acts at the base of marine food webs that supply the primary protein of more than a billion people. Only cutting CO2 emissions slows it; surface-ocean chemistry takes millennia to recover on its own.
published.name: Ocean Acidification

assessment.summary: A present, quantified fiscal squeeze — record external debt stock, the largest net outflow from developing countries in half a century, and 3.4 billion people in states paying more in interest than they spend on health or education — that is tightening as borrowing costs climb: Group of Seven ten-year yields are at their highest in nearly two decades and the global primary deficit is widening rather than closing. A synchronised multi-country default wave remains the tail risk.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing and tightening; the World Bank's International Debt Report tracks the position annually, and the IMF's October 2026 Fiscal Monitor expects global public debt to exceed 100 percent of global GDP by 2030, with the effective average interest cost of government financing rising from 2.3 percent in 2021 to 3.7 percent by 2031.

claims.text: Developing countries paid out $741 billion more in principal and interest on their external debt than they received in new financing between 2022 and 2024, and paid a record $415 billion in interest alone in 2024 (International Debt Report 2025, published 3 December 2025).

The combined external debt of low- and middle-income countries hit an all-time high of $8.9 trillion in 2024, including $1.2 trillion owed by the 78 mainly low-income countries eligible to borrow from the World Bank's International Development Association; developing countries restructured $90 billion in external debt in 2024, more than at any time since 2010.

More than 3.4 billion people now live in countries that spend more on interest payments than on health or education — 100 million more than the previous year — and debt service payments by developing countries soared by $74 billion in a single year, from $847 billion to $921 billion (Confronting the Debt Crisis: 11 Actions to Unlock Sustainable Financing, launched 27 June 2025).

Global public debt rose to just under 94 percent of GDP in 2025 and is set to reach 100 percent by 2029, one year earlier than projected in April 2025 (IMF Fiscal Monitor, April 2026: Fiscal Policy under Pressure: High Debt, Rising Risks).

The IMF's October 2026 Fiscal Monitor expects global public debt to exceed 100 percent of global gross domestic product by 2030; the Group of Seven's average 10-year government bond yield increased by over 1 percentage point between February and September 2026, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades; the effective average interest cost of government financing is projected to rise from 2.3 percent in 2021 to 3.7 percent by 2031; and the global primary deficit is about 3.3 percent of GDP in 2026, against the roughly 2.6 percent it would have to be cut to in order to stabilize the global debt-to-GDP ratio this year.

In just three years, interest payments have increased by almost half - from about 2 to nearly 3 percent of GDP - amounting to trillions of dollars globally that cannot go to education, infrastructure, or other priorities, and debt was already on track to reach World War II-era levels by 2028 (IMF Annual Report 2026).

published.description: A growing share of the world's governments owe more in debt service than they can pay without cutting health, education, and climate spending. The combined external debt of low- and middle-income countries hit an all-time high of $8.9 trillion in 2024, and between 2022 and 2024 those countries paid out $741 billion more in principal and interest than they received in new financing — the largest such gap in at least 50 years. More than 3.4 billion people live in countries that spend more on interest payments than on health or education, and interest has climbed from about 2 to nearly 3 percent of global GDP in three years. The strain is not confined to poorer economies: global public debt reached just under 94 percent of GDP in 2025, the IMF expects it to pass 100 percent by 2030, and Group of Seven ten-year yields rose more than a percentage point between February and September 2026 to their highest level in nearly two decades. The escalation pathway runs from isolated sovereign defaults to a synchronised wave of restructurings, capital flight, and a lost decade of development spending across dozens of countries at once.
published.name: Sovereign Debt Distress

assessment.summary: A steadily growing, already-tracked debris population in Earth orbit carries a real and rising risk of a self-sustaining collision cascade severe enough to disable critical satellite infrastructure.
assessment.timeframe: Debris accumulation is continuous and tracked in real time; a runaway cascade has no predicted date but becomes more likely as orbital object density rises.

claims.text: NASA's Orbital Debris Program Office states more than 25,000 tracked objects larger than 10 cm orbit Earth, with an estimated 500,000 objects between 1 and 10 cm, and more than 100 million objects larger than 1 mm; as of January 2022 the total mass of orbiting material exceeded 9,000 metric tons.
NASA states the International Space Station maneuvers to avoid a tracked object when the estimated collision probability exceeds 1 in 10,000, which occurs about once a year on average.

NASA describes the Kessler syndrome as a domino effect that can result when objects in intersecting orbits collide at thousands of miles per hour, generating debris that raises the odds of further collisions.

The Satellite Box Score in NASA's Orbital Debris Quarterly News (Volume 30, Issue 1 & 2, July 2026) lists 33,098 objects in Earth orbit cataloged by the U.S. Space Surveillance Network as of 4 May 2026 — 18,189 spacecraft, active and defunct, and 14,909 spent rocket bodies and other cataloged debris.

NASA's Orbital Debris Program Office states that because the orbital debris population follows a power-law size distribution, there is far more millimeter-sized debris (on the order of 100 million) than large, trackable objects (approximately 50,000), so the likelihood of non-catastrophic but mission-ending damage from millimeter-sized debris is orders of magnitude greater than that of an accidental collision with a large, trackable object.

published.description: Decades of launches, spent rocket stages, defunct satellites, and past collisions have left a large and growing population of debris in Earth orbit. As the density of objects in low Earth orbit rises, so does the risk of a cascading chain reaction of collisions — the 'Kessler syndrome' — that could render whole orbital bands too hazardous for satellites and crewed spacecraft for generations, threatening the GPS, communications, weather, and scientific infrastructure the world now depends on. The US Space Surveillance Network now catalogs more than 33,000 objects in orbit, over half of them spacecraft, and NASA estimates on the order of 100 million fragments larger than a millimetre that are too small to track yet still capable of ending a mission. Spacecraft including the International Space Station maneuver away from tracked objects when the collision probability exceeds 1 in 10,000.
published.name: Space Debris and Kessler Syndrome

assessment.summary: A continent-scale disaster with extremely low annual probability, continuously monitored, and with no current signs of unrest beyond background levels.
assessment.timeframe: No reliable short-term forecast. The three largest past eruptions occurred ~2.1M, ~1.3M, and ~0.64M years ago.

claims.text: The USGS estimates the yearly probability of another Yellowstone caldera-forming eruption at roughly 1 in 730,000 (0.00014%), based on averaging the intervals between the three past major eruptions.

USGS states Yellowstone's three caldera-forming eruptions were the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff (~2.1 million years ago), the Mesa Falls Tuff (~1.3 million years ago), and the Lava Creek Tuff (~640,000 years ago).
The USGS states there is no evidence that a catastrophic eruption at Yellowstone is imminent, and that such events are unlikely to occur in the next few centuries.

The Yellowstone Volcano Observatory's 1 September 2026 monthly update gives the current Volcano Alert Level as NORMAL and the current Aviation Color Code as GREEN, and reports 61 earthquakes located in the Yellowstone National Park region during August 2026, the largest a magnitude 2.0 micro earthquake.

published.description: A large caldera system beneath Yellowstone National Park capable of a 'supereruption' that would blanket much of North America in ash and inject climate-altering aerosols into the stratosphere. Eruptions on that scale are extraordinarily rare: the USGS puts the yearly probability of another caldera-forming eruption at roughly 1 in 730,000 and states there is no evidence one is imminent, or likely within the next few centuries. The Yellowstone Volcano Observatory holds the volcano at its lowest status — Volcano Alert Level NORMAL, Aviation Color Code GREEN — with seismicity at background levels and caldera uplift of about a centimetre or less over recent months.
published.name: Yellowstone Supervolcano
